title: Exponential Functions & Growth
blurb: Growth and decay factors from percent rates, the shape of an exponential graph and its asymptote, why exponential growth eventually beats any linear growth, and building a model from a description, a table, or two data points.
buildsOn: Geometric sequences from Unit 3 — the same repeated multiplication, now with the exponent free to run continuously — and the linear models of Unit 4, which this unit races against.

lessons.title: Growth & Decay Factors
lessons.concreteComparison: Two savings accounts, both starting at $100\,000$₮. One adds $10\,000$₮ a year. The other adds ten percent a year. After one year they are identical. After thirty years the second holds nearly twice the first — because adding a fixed amount and multiplying by a fixed factor are different engines, and only one of them accelerates.
lessons.objective: Recognise a constant percent rate of change, convert a percent to a growth or decay factor, write the model $y = a \cdot b^{x}$, and interpret $a$ and $b$ in context.
concept: **Linear adds; exponential multiplies.** A linear model changes by the same AMOUNT each step: $+900$₮ per kilometre, whatever the total so far. An exponential model changes by the same PERCENT each step: $+10\%$ per year, which is a bigger and bigger amount as the total grows. That difference is the whole unit.

**The model.** Written $y = a \cdot b^{x}$, where $a$ is the starting value — the output at $x = 0$, since $b^0 = 1$ — and $b$ is the factor applied once per step. The variable sits in the EXPONENT, which is what makes the function exponential rather than merely curved.

**Converting a percent to a factor.** Growing by $p\%$ means keeping everything and adding $p\%$, so $b = 1 + \frac{p}{100}$: growth of $8\%$ gives $b = 1.08$. Decaying by $p\%$ means keeping the rest, so $b = 1 - \frac{p}{100}$: a loss of $15\%$ gives $b = 0.85$. The factor is always what SURVIVES one step, never what is gained or lost.

**Reading the factor backwards.** Given $b = 1.06$, the growth rate is $6\%$. Given $b = 0.92$, the quantity keeps $92\%$ and therefore loses $8\%$. Given $b = 2$, it doubles — a $100\%$ increase, which is worth pausing on: doubling is $+100\%$, not $+200\%$.

**Percent changes compound; they do not add.** Three years of $10\%$ growth multiplies by $1.1^3 = 1.331$, a $33.1\%$ increase — not $30\%$. Two years of $12\%$ decay leaves $0.88^2 = 0.7744$, so $22.56\%$ is lost, not $24\%$. Each step acts on the result of the last, and that is exactly why the curve bends.

**Spotting the model from a table.** Compute DIFFERENCES between consecutive outputs; constant means linear. If they are not constant, compute RATIOS; constant means exponential. This is the same two-step test as Unit 3's sequences, now applied to any table of values.
lessons.keyIdea: $y = a \cdot b^{x}$: $a$ is the starting value, $b$ is the factor per step. Growth of $p\%$ gives $b = 1 + p/100$; decay gives $b = 1 - p/100$. The factor is what survives, and repeated steps compound.

facts.title: The exponential model
facts.latex: y = a \cdot b^{x}, \qquad a = \text{start}, \quad b = \text{factor per step}
facts.explanation: At x = 0 the factor is b⁰ = 1, so y = a — the starting value.

facts.title: Percent to factor
facts.explanation: The factor is what SURVIVES one step. Losing 15% gives 0.85, not 0.15.

facts.title: Compounding, not adding
facts.explanation: Each step acts on the previous result, so three years of 10% is a 33.1% rise.

workedExamples.statement: A town of $40\,000$ people grows $3\%$ a year. Write the model and find the population after $5$ years.
workedExamples.solution: **Find the factor.** Growing $3\%$ means keeping everything and adding three percent:$$b = 1 + 0.03 = 1.03.$$**Write the model.** With $a = 40\,000$ as the starting population and $t$ in years,$$P(t) = 40\,000 \cdot (1.03)^{t}.$$Check the start: $P(0) = 40\,000 \cdot 1 = 40\,000$ ✓**After 5 years.**$$P(5) = 40\,000 \times 1.03^{5} = 40\,000 \times 1.159274074 \approx 46\,371.$$About $46\,371$ people.**Not a fifteen percent rise.** Five years of $3\%$ gives $15.93\%$ growth, not $15\%$, because each year's increase is computed on a larger population than the last.

workedExamples.statement: A car bought for $32\,000\,000$₮ loses $18\%$ of its value each year. Write the model and find its value after $4$ years.
workedExamples.solution: **Find the factor.** Losing $18\%$ means KEEPING $82\%$:$$b = 1 - 0.18 = 0.82.$$Since $0 < b < 1$, this is decay — the values fall.**Model.**$$V(t) = 32\,000\,000 \cdot (0.82)^{t}.$$**After 4 years.**$$0.82^{4} = 0.45212176, \qquad V(4) = 32\,000\,000 \times 0.45212176 = 14\,467\,896.32.$$The car is worth about $14\,467\,896$₮.**Why the losses do not simply add.** Four years at $18\%$ leaves $45.2\%$, not $100 - 4(18) = 28\%$. Each year's loss is taken from a smaller base, so the value decays toward zero without ever quite reaching it — a linear model would have hit zero at year $5.6$ and gone negative after.

workedExamples.statement: Decide whether each table is linear or exponential, and give its model. Table A: $(0, 5), (1, 8), (2, 11), (3, 14)$. Table B: $(0, 5), (1, 15), (2, 45), (3, 135)$.
workedExamples.solution: **Table A — differences first.**$$8 - 5 = 3, \qquad 11 - 8 = 3, \qquad 14 - 11 = 3.$$Constant, so it is **linear** with slope $3$ and starting value $5$:$$y = 3x + 5.$$**Table B — differences.**$$15 - 5 = 10, \qquad 45 - 15 = 30, \qquad 135 - 45 = 90.$$Not constant, so not linear. **Now ratios.**$$\frac{15}{5} = 3, \qquad \frac{45}{15} = 3, \qquad \frac{135}{45} = 3.$$Constant, so it is **exponential** with $a = 5$ and $b = 3$:$$y = 5 \cdot 3^{x}.$$Check at $x = 3$: $5 \cdot 27 = 135$ ✓**The habit.** Differences, then ratios. A table that fails both is neither, and no model from this unit will fit it.

workedExamples.statement: A model reads $N = 250 \cdot (1.4)^{t}$. State the starting value, the percent growth per period, and the value after $3$ periods. Then say how the answer would change if the model were $N = 250 \cdot (0.6)^{t}$.
workedExamples.solution: **Starting value.** At $t = 0$: $N = 250 \cdot 1 = 250$.**Percent growth.** The factor is $1.4 = 1 + 0.4$, so the quantity grows $40\%$ per period.**After 3 periods.**$$N(3) = 250 \times 1.4^{3} = 250 \times 2.744 = 686.$$**The decay version.** A factor of $0.6 = 1 - 0.4$ means the quantity LOSES $40\%$ per period, keeping $60\%$:$$N(3) = 250 \times 0.6^{3} = 250 \times 0.216 = 54.$$**The symmetry that is not there.** Growing $40\%$ and then shrinking $40\%$ does NOT return you to the start: $250 \times 1.4 \times 0.6 = 210$, not $250$. The two percentages are taken from different bases, which is one of the most consistently surprising facts in this unit.

commonMistakes.text: Using 0.15 as the factor for a 15% loss.
commonMistakes.correction: The factor is what SURVIVES: 1 − 0.15 = 0.85. Using 0.15 models keeping only fifteen percent, a 85% loss.

commonMistakes.text: Treating five years of 3% growth as a 15% rise.
commonMistakes.correction: Percent changes compound: 1.03⁵ = 1.1593, a 15.93% rise. Multiplying the rate by the number of years is the linear answer to an exponential question.

commonMistakes.text: Applying the arithmetic-sequence formula to a table with constant ratios.
commonMistakes.correction: Test differences first; if they drift, test ratios. A constant ratio means y = a·bˣ, and no linear model will fit.

commonMistakes.text: Assuming a 40% rise followed by a 40% fall returns to the start.
commonMistakes.correction: 1.4 × 0.6 = 0.84, so you end 16% down. The two percentages are taken from different bases.

tryIt.statement: A colony of $600$ bacteria grows $25\%$ each hour. Write the model and find the count after $3$ hours.
tryIt.solution: The factor is $1.25$, so $N(t) = 600 \cdot (1.25)^{t}$. After $3$ hours: $600 \times 1.953125 = 1171.875$, about $1172$ bacteria.

tryIt.statement: A drug's concentration falls $30\%$ every hour from an initial $80$ mg. Write the model and find the amount after $2$ hours.
tryIt.solution: Keeping $70\%$ gives a factor of $0.7$, so $C(t) = 80 \cdot (0.7)^{t}$. After $2$ hours: $80 \times 0.49 = 39.2$ mg.

tryIt.statement: Is $(0, 7), (1, 21), (2, 63), (3, 189)$ linear or exponential? Give the model.
tryIt.solution: Differences $14, 42, 126$ are not constant. Ratios $\frac{21}{7} = \frac{63}{21} = \frac{189}{63} = 3$ are, so it is exponential with $a = 7$ and $b = 3$: $y = 7 \cdot 3^{x}$. Check at $x = 3$: $7 \times 27 = 189$ ✓

steps.title: Adding a fixed amount, or multiplying by a fixed factor
steps.body: A linear model changes by the same AMOUNT each step. An exponential model changes by the same PERCENT — which is a bigger and bigger amount as the quantity grows. Two engines, and only one accelerates.
beats: Exponential: $+10\%$ a year — a growing amount
Year 1 they agree; year 30 they do not

steps.title: The curve of repeated multiplication
steps.teach: $y = a \cdot b^{x}$. Change the base and watch the shape: above $1$ it climbs faster and faster; below $1$ it falls toward zero without ever reaching it.

steps.title: The factor is what survives one step
steps.body: Growing $8\%$ keeps everything and adds eight percent: $b = 1.08$. Losing $15\%$ keeps eighty-five percent: $b = 0.85$. The factor is never the percentage itself — it is what remains after the step.

steps.title: What is the factor?
steps.prompt: A population falls by $12\%$ each year. What is $b$ in the model $y = a \cdot b^{t}$?
steps.explanation: Losing $12\%$ means keeping $88\%$, so $b = 1 - 0.12 = 0.88$. Check on a population of $500$: after one year $500 \times 0.88 = 440$, a loss of $60$, which is indeed $12\%$ of $500$ ✓. A factor of $0.12$ would model losing $88\%$.

steps.title: Percent changes multiply, they do not add
steps.body: Three years of $10\%$ growth is $1.1^3 = 1.331$ — a $33.1\%$ rise, not $30\%$. Each year's increase is computed on the previous year's total, and that extra bit is where the curve comes from.

steps.title: How much after two years?
steps.prompt: A quantity of $1000$ grows $20\%$ a year. What is it worth after two years?
steps.explanation: $1000 \times 1.2 = 1200$ after one year, then $1200 \times 1.2 = 1440$ after two. Equivalently $1000 \times 1.2^2 = 1440$. The answer $1400$ comes from adding $20\% + 20\% = 40\%$ — the linear answer, which misses the $40$ earned on the first year's gain.

steps.title: Differences, then ratios
steps.body: Given a table, subtract consecutive outputs. Constant → linear. Not constant → divide consecutive outputs instead. Constant → exponential. The same two-step test you used on sequences in Unit 3.

steps.title: A 40% rise and a 40% fall lose you money
steps.body: Gain forty percent, then lose forty percent: $1.4 \times 0.6 = 0.84$. You end sixteen percent DOWN, not level. The rise was taken on the small number and the fall on the large one — which is why percentage changes must always be multiplied, never added.

steps.title: What you now own
points: Linear adds a fixed amount; exponential multiplies by a fixed factor
$y = a \cdot b^{x}$: $a$ is the start, $b$ is the factor per step
Percent changes **compound** — never multiply the rate by the periods
Classify a table by differences first, then ratios

lessons.title: Graphing Exponential Functions
lessons.concreteComparison: A rumour spreads through a school. On day one two people know it; by the end of the week it is everywhere. Plotted, that is not a ramp — it is a curve that lies almost flat and then turns almost vertical. Recognising that shape on sight tells you what kind of model you are looking at before you compute anything.
lessons.objective: Graph $y = a \cdot b^{x}$ from a table of values, identify the $y$-intercept and the horizontal asymptote, and describe the end behaviour of a growth curve and a decay curve.
concept: **The vertical intercept is always the starting value.** Since $b^0 = 1$ for any positive base, $y = a \cdot b^{0} = a$. Every exponential curve of this form crosses the vertical axis at its starting value, and it does so exactly once.

**There is no horizontal intercept.** A positive $a$ times a positive power is always positive, so the curve NEVER touches the horizontal axis. It approaches $y = 0$ without arriving — the axis is a horizontal ASYMPTOTE. This is the sharpest visual difference from a line, which crosses the axis exactly once.

**Growth and decay are mirror images.** For $b > 1$ the curve rises to the right and flattens toward the axis on the left. For $0 < b < 1$ it does the opposite: falls to the right and climbs steeply on the left. Both hug the axis at one end and run away at the other.

**Read the end behaviour in words.** For $y = 3 \cdot 2^{x}$: as $x$ grows large the output grows without bound; as $x$ becomes very negative the output approaches zero. For a decay curve the two statements swap. Saying which end approaches zero is usually the mark on offer.

**A table makes the shape obvious.** Compute a few values either side of zero. For $y = 2^{x}$: at $x = -2$ it is $\frac{1}{4}$, at $x = 0$ it is $1$, at $x = 3$ it is $8$, at $x = 6$ it is $64$. Negative inputs give small positive outputs — never negative ones — which is the fact that makes the asymptote visible.

**In context, the asymptote has a meaning.** A cooling cup of tea approaches room temperature; a drug's concentration approaches zero. The horizontal asymptote is usually the value the situation settles toward but never quite reaches, and naming it is part of interpreting the model.
lessons.keyIdea: $y = a \cdot b^{x}$ crosses the vertical axis at $a$, never crosses the horizontal axis, and approaches $y = 0$ at one end while growing without bound at the other.

facts.title: The intercept
facts.explanation: Any positive base to the power zero is 1, so the curve always meets the vertical axis at its starting value.

facts.title: The asymptote
facts.latex: a > 0, \ b > 0 \ \Rightarrow\ y > 0 \ \text{ for every } x
facts.explanation: The output can get arbitrarily close to zero but never reaches it — so there is no x-intercept.

facts.title: Negative exponents are small, not negative
facts.explanation: A negative exponent flips to a reciprocal. The result stays positive, which is why the curve stays above the axis.

workedExamples.statement: Make a table for $y = 2^{x}$ at $x = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3$ and describe the graph.
workedExamples.solution: **Table.**$$2^{-2} = \frac{1}{4}, \quad 2^{-1} = \frac{1}{2}, \quad 2^{0} = 1, \quad 2^{1} = 2, \quad 2^{2} = 4, \quad 2^{3} = 8.$$**The shape.** Reading left to right, the outputs are tiny and positive, then cross the vertical axis at $1$, then double with every step. The curve is almost flat on the left and almost vertical on the right.**Key features.** The $y$-intercept is $1$ (which is $a$). There is no $x$-intercept — every output listed is positive, and that is true for every input, since a power of $2$ is never zero or negative.**End behaviour.** As $x \to \infty$ the output grows without bound; as $x \to -\infty$ it approaches $0$, so $y = 0$ is a horizontal asymptote.

workedExamples.statement: Describe the graph of $y = 5 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{x}$, including its intercept, asymptote and end behaviour.
workedExamples.solution: **Intercept.** At $x = 0$: $y = 5 \cdot 1 = 5$, so the curve crosses the vertical axis at $(0, 5)$.**Values.** At $x = 1$: $2.5$. At $x = 2$: $1.25$. At $x = 3$: $0.625$. Each step right halves the output.**Left of zero.** At $x = -1$: $5 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-1} = 5 \cdot 2 = 10$. At $x = -2$: $5 \cdot 4 = 20$. A negative exponent flips the fraction, so the curve climbs steeply to the left.**Asymptote and end behaviour.** Since $0 < b < 1$, this is decay: as $x \to \infty$ the output approaches $0$ without reaching it, so $y = 0$ is the horizontal asymptote. As $x \to -\infty$ the output grows without bound.**The mirror.** This is the growth picture reflected left-to-right, which is what $b < 1$ always does.

workedExamples.statement: Two functions: $f(x) = 3 \cdot 2^{x}$ and $g(x) = 3 \cdot 4^{x}$. Compare their graphs.
workedExamples.solution: **Same intercept.** Both have $a = 3$, so both cross the vertical axis at $(0, 3)$ — the base does not affect where the curve starts.**Different steepness.** Compare a few values:$$f(1) = 6, \quad g(1) = 12; \qquad f(2) = 12, \quad g(2) = 48; \qquad f(3) = 24, \quad g(3) = 192.$$The larger base climbs far faster — by $x = 3$, $g$ is eight times $f$.**On the left.** At $x = -2$: $f(-2) = \frac{3}{4} = 0.75$ and $g(-2) = \frac{3}{16} = 0.1875$. The larger base also approaches the asymptote FASTER going left, hugging the axis more tightly.**Summary.** A bigger base makes the curve steeper in both directions: it rises more sharply to the right and flattens onto the asymptote more quickly to the left. Both still share the intercept $3$ and the asymptote $y = 0$.

workedExamples.statement: A cup of tea cools so that its temperature above room temperature is $T = 60 \cdot (0.8)^{m}$ degrees, with $m$ in minutes and room temperature $20°$C. Sketch the behaviour and say what the asymptote means.
workedExamples.solution: **What the model gives.** $T$ is the temperature ABOVE room temperature, so the actual temperature is $20 + T$.**Values.** At $m = 0$: $T = 60$, so the tea is at $80°$C. At $m = 5$: $60 \times 0.32768 = 19.66$, so about $39.7°$C. At $m = 15$: $60 \times 0.035184 = 2.11$, so about $22.1°$C.**The asymptote.** As $m$ grows, $T \to 0$ — so the actual temperature approaches $20°$C, room temperature, without ever quite reaching it. That is what the horizontal asymptote MEANS here: the tea cannot cool below the room, and it gets arbitrarily close.**Why the model is realistic.** The tea cools fastest when it is hottest, because each minute removes twenty percent of a shrinking gap. A linear cooling model would have the tea reaching room temperature at a specific time and then continuing to cool below it, which is physically wrong.

commonMistakes.text: Claiming an exponential graph has an x-intercept.
commonMistakes.correction: a·bˣ with a and b positive is always positive. The curve approaches the axis but never crosses it — that is the asymptote.
A negative exponent means a reciprocal: 2⁻³ = 1/8, positive and small. That is exactly why the curve stays above the axis on the left.

commonMistakes.text: Thinking a bigger base moves the y-intercept.
commonMistakes.correction: The intercept is a, whatever the base. Both 3·2ˣ and 3·4ˣ cross at (0, 3); the base only changes how steeply they leave it.

commonMistakes.text: Drawing an exponential curve as a straight line through the plotted points.
commonMistakes.correction: Join the points with a smooth curve. The whole content of the model is that the rate of change is not constant.

tryIt.statement: For $y = 4 \cdot 3^{x}$, give the $y$-intercept and the values at $x = 2$ and $x = -1$.
tryIt.solution: The intercept is $a = 4$, at $(0, 4)$. At $x = 2$: $4 \times 9 = 36$. At $x = -1$: $4 \times \frac{1}{3} = \frac{4}{3}$ — small and positive, not negative.

Since $0 < b < 1$ this is decay. As $x \to \infty$ the output approaches $0$ (the horizontal asymptote $y = 0$) without reaching it; as $x \to -\infty$ it grows without bound. Check: at $x = 10$ it is $0.0977$, at $x = -3$ it is $800$.

tryIt.statement: Which grows faster for large $x$: $y = 50 \cdot 1.5^{x}$ or $y = 5 \cdot 3^{x}$? Check at $x = 2$ and $x = 8$.
tryIt.solution: At $x = 2$: the first gives $50 \times 2.25 = 112.5$, the second $5 \times 9 = 45$ — the first leads. At $x = 8$: the first gives $50 \times 25.63 \approx 1281$, the second $5 \times 6561 = 32\,805$ — the second has overtaken decisively. The larger BASE wins eventually, whatever the starting values.

steps.title: The curve always starts at a
steps.body: Any positive base to the power zero is $1$, so $y = a \cdot b^{0} = a$. Every exponential of this form crosses the vertical axis at its starting value — the base has nothing to do with it.

steps.title: Same start, different steepness
steps.teach: Change the base and watch. The intercept never moves — it is $a$ — but a larger base makes the curve leave it far more sharply, and hug the asymptote more tightly on the other side.

steps.title: A table for 2 to the x
It never crosses the horizontal axis
steps.body: A positive $a$ times a positive power is positive, always. So the curve approaches $y = 0$ and never arrives — the axis is a horizontal ASYMPTOTE. A line crosses the axis exactly once; an exponential never does.

steps.title: What is the value here?
steps.explanation: A negative exponent means a reciprocal, not a negative number: $3^{-2} = \frac{1}{3^{2}} = \frac{1}{9}$. Small and positive — which is exactly why an exponential curve stays above the axis for negative inputs instead of dropping below it.

steps.title: Growth rises right; decay rises left
steps.body: For $b > 1$ the curve climbs to the right and flattens onto the axis going left. For $0 < b < 1$ it does the reverse. They are mirror images, and both hug the axis at one end.

steps.title: Which end approaches zero?
steps.prompt: For $y = 7 \cdot (0.4)^{x}$, at which end does the curve approach the horizontal asymptote?
steps.explanation: The base $0.4$ is below $1$, so each step right multiplies by less than one and the output shrinks toward zero. Check: $y(5) = 7 \times 0.01024 = 0.072$, already tiny. Going LEFT, negative exponents flip the fraction and the output grows: $y(-2) = 7 \times 6.25 = 43.75$.

steps.title: The asymptote usually means something
steps.body: Tea cools toward room temperature. A drug clears toward zero concentration. The horizontal asymptote is the value the situation settles toward but never quite reaches — and naming it is part of reading the model.

steps.title: Join the points with a curve, not a ruler
steps.body: The entire content of an exponential model is that the rate of change is not constant. Drawing straight segments between plotted points draws a shape the model does not have — and loses the mark for the graph.

steps.title: What you now own
points: The $y$-intercept is $a$, whatever the base
There is **no** $x$-intercept — $y = 0$ is a horizontal asymptote
A negative exponent gives a small **positive** value, not a negative one
$b > 1$ rises to the right; $0 < b < 1$ falls to the right
In context the asymptote is what the situation approaches but never reaches

lessons.title: Linear vs Exponential: Who Wins
lessons.concreteComparison: Offered a job at $1$₮ on day one, doubling daily for a month, or a flat $1\,000\,000$₮ a day — most people take the million. By day $25$ the doubling wage passes it, and by day $31$ it pays over a billion tugriks in that single day. Linear growth is steady and legible. Exponential growth is patient and then overwhelming.
lessons.objective: Compare linear and exponential models numerically and graphically, locate the crossover, and state why an exponential quantity eventually exceeds any linear one.
concept: **Exponential always wins eventually.** This is F-LE.3, and it holds without exception: for any linear function $mx + c$ and any exponential $a \cdot b^{x}$ with $b > 1$ and $a > 0$, there is some input beyond which the exponential is larger and stays larger. Not usually, not typically — always. The only question is WHEN.

**But it can start far behind.** $y = 2^{x}$ begins at $1$ while $y = 1000x$ begins climbing by a thousand a step. For a long stretch the line is far ahead. Then the curve catches it and the gap reverses permanently — and the reversal, once it starts, is fast.

**Why the curve must win.** Each step of a linear model ADDS $m$, a fixed amount. Each step of an exponential MULTIPLIES by $b$, and multiplying a large number by $b > 1$ adds a large amount. So the exponential's step size keeps growing while the linear one never changes. Once the exponential's step exceeds $m$, it gains ground every step thereafter and never gives it back.

**Finding the crossover.** In IM1 you locate it by table or by graph — trying values until the winner flips, then narrowing. Solving $2^{x} = 1000x$ exactly requires logarithms, which arrive in IM2. Being able to say "between $x = 13$ and $x = 14$" from a table is the expected answer here, and it is a genuinely useful skill.

**Which model fits which situation.** Ask what stays constant. A wage of $900$₮ per extra kilometre, a candle losing $4$ cm an hour, a fee per item — constant AMOUNT, so linear. Interest at $6\%$, a population growing $3\%$, a drug clearing $30\%$ an hour — constant PERCENT, so exponential. The phrase "per year" appears in both; what matters is whether it is followed by a unit or a percent sign.
lessons.keyIdea: An exponential with base above $1$ eventually exceeds ANY linear function, because its step size grows while the line's stays fixed. It may start far behind, and the crossover is found by table or graph.

facts.title: The eventual-dominance fact
facts.latex: b > 1 \ \Longrightarrow\ a b^{x} > mx + c \ \text{ for all large enough } x
facts.explanation: F-LE.3. True for every linear function, no matter how steep — only the crossover point changes.

facts.title: Why
facts.explanation: The exponential's own step size grows without bound, so it must overtake a fixed step eventually.

facts.title: Which model to choose
facts.explanation: '+900₮ per km' is linear. '+6% per year' is exponential. Read what follows the 'per'.

workedExamples.statement: Compare $L(x) = 100x + 50$ with $E(x) = 2 \cdot 3^{x}$ at $x = 1, 3, 5$ and $7$. Where does the exponential overtake?
workedExamples.solution: **Evaluate both.**$$x = 1: \quad L = 150, \qquad E = 6.$$$$x = 3: \quad L = 350, \qquad E = 54.$$$$x = 5: \quad L = 550, \qquad E = 486.$$$$x = 7: \quad L = 750, \qquad E = 4374.$$**The crossover.** The line leads at $x = 5$ ($550$ against $486$) but has been overtaken by $x = 7$. Narrowing: at $x = 6$, $L = 650$ and $E = 1458$ — the exponential has already won. So the crossover lies between $x = 5$ and $x = 6$.**After that.** The gap only widens: at $x = 10$, $L = 1050$ while $E = 118\,098$ — over a hundred times larger. Once the curve passes the line it never returns.

workedExamples.statement: A job pays $1$₮ on day $1$, doubling each day. Another pays $1\,000\,000$₮ flat per day. Compare the DAILY pay on days $10$, $20$, $25$ and $31$.
workedExamples.solution: **Models.** Doubling: $D(n) = 2^{\,n-1}$ tugriks on day $n$. Flat: $F(n) = 1\,000\,000$ every day.**Day 10.** $D = 2^{9} = 512$₮ against $1\,000\,000$₮. The flat wage is nearly two thousand times better.**Day 20.** $D = 2^{19} = 524\,288$₮ — still behind, but only just.**Day 21.** $D = 2^{20} = 1\,048\,576$₮ — the doubling wage has overtaken.**Day 31.** $D = 2^{30} = 1\,073\,741\,824$₮, over a billion tugriks in a single day, against the same one million.**The point.** For twenty days the flat wage looks obviously better, and it is. Then eleven more days turn a $1$₮ start into more than a thousand times the flat rate. Nothing about the first twenty days hints at this — which is precisely why exponential growth is so consistently underestimated.

workedExamples.statement: Decide whether each situation is linear or exponential, and say why. (a) A phone plan charges $18\,000$₮ plus $40$₮ a minute. (b) A savings account pays $7\%$ interest a year. (c) A tank loses $12$ litres a minute. (d) A rumour: each person who knows it tells two new people every hour.
workedExamples.solution: **(a) Linear.** Each extra minute adds the same $40$₮, whatever the bill so far — a constant AMOUNT. Model: $C = 40m + 18\,000$.**(b) Exponential.** Seven percent of a growing balance is a growing amount — a constant PERCENT. Model: $B = P \cdot (1.07)^{t}$.**(c) Linear.** Twelve litres leave every minute regardless of how full the tank is — a constant amount. Model: $V = V_0 - 12t$.**(d) Exponential.** The number of new tellers is proportional to how many already know, so the count multiplies each hour — with each person telling two new people, the total triples: $N = N_0 \cdot 3^{t}$.**The test.** Ask what stays the same from step to step. A fixed quantity of something means linear; a fixed proportion of the current total means exponential.

workedExamples.statement: Investment A starts at $5\,000\,000$₮ and adds $400\,000$₮ a year. Investment B starts at $3\,000\,000$₮ and grows $12\%$ a year. Which is worth more after $5$ years? After $15$?
workedExamples.solution: **Models.**$$A(t) = 5\,000\,000 + 400\,000t, \qquad B(t) = 3\,000\,000 \cdot (1.12)^{t}.$$**After 5 years.**$$A(5) = 5\,000\,000 + 2\,000\,000 = 7\,000\,000.$$$$B(5) = 3\,000\,000 \times 1.7623416832 = 5\,287\,025.$$**A leads**, by over $1.7$ million.**After 15 years.**$$A(15) = 5\,000\,000 + 6\,000\,000 = 11\,000\,000.$$$$B(15) = 3\,000\,000 \times 5.4735665 = 16\,420\,700.$$**B leads**, and by a growing margin.**Crossover.** Testing between: at $t = 10$, $A = 9\,000\,000$ and $B = 3\,000\,000 \times 3.1058 = 9\,317\,467$ — B has just passed. At $t = 9$, $A = 8\,600\,000$ and $B = 8\,319\,167$ — A still leads. So the crossover is between years $9$ and $10$.**The advice.** For a short horizon A is better and safer to predict. Past about ten years B dominates, and the longer the horizon the more decisively — which is the whole argument for starting to save early.

commonMistakes.text: Concluding the linear model wins because it leads over the range you checked.
commonMistakes.correction: Check further out. An exponential with base above 1 always overtakes eventually — the table just has not reached the crossover yet.

commonMistakes.text: Reading '7% per year' as a constant amount and modelling it linearly.
commonMistakes.correction: A percent of a changing total is a changing amount. Constant percent means exponential; only a constant quantity per step is linear.

commonMistakes.text: Trying to solve 2ˣ = 1000x algebraically in IM1.
commonMistakes.correction: That needs logarithms (IM2). Here, locate the crossover by table or graph and state the interval it falls in.

commonMistakes.text: Assuming a steeper line must beat a shallow curve.
commonMistakes.correction: Slope is irrelevant to the eventual outcome. A line of slope one million still loses to 2ˣ — it just takes longer.

tryIt.statement: Compare $L(x) = 20x$ with $E(x) = 2^{x}$ at $x = 4, 6$ and $8$. Where is the crossover?
tryIt.solution: At $x = 4$: $L = 80$, $E = 16$ — the line leads. At $x = 6$: $L = 120$, $E = 64$ — still the line. At $x = 8$: $L = 160$, $E = 256$ — the exponential has won. Checking $x = 7$: $L = 140$, $E = 128$ — the line still leads, so the crossover is between $x = 7$ and $x = 8$.

tryIt.statement: Classify: (a) a taxi charging $700$₮ per km; (b) a bacterial culture doubling every $20$ minutes.
tryIt.solution: (a) **Linear** — each kilometre adds the same $700$₮, a constant amount. (b) **Exponential** — the population multiplies by $2$ each period, a constant factor, so the increase grows as the culture grows.

tryIt.statement: A city of $200\,000$ grows $2\%$ a year; another of $260\,000$ grows by $3000$ people a year. Which is larger after $10$ years? After $30$?
tryIt.solution: After $10$: the first is $200\,000 \times 1.2190 = 243\,799$; the second is $260\,000 + 30\,000 = 290\,000$ — the **second** leads. After $30$: the first is $200\,000 \times 1.8114 = 362\,272$; the second is $260\,000 + 90\,000 = 350\,000$ — the **first** has overtaken.

steps.title: The curve always wins — eventually
steps.body: For ANY linear function and any exponential with base above $1$, there is a point past which the exponential is larger and stays larger. Not usually — always. The only open question is when.
beats: Slope of the line: irrelevant to the outcome
A line of slope $1\,000\,000$ still loses
After it, the gap widens without limit

steps.title: Behind, level, then gone
steps.teach: A line and a curve on the same axes. The line leads for a long stretch, they meet, and then the curve pulls away and never comes back. Drag the parameters and watch the crossover move — but never disappear.

steps.title: A line and a curve, side by side
The step size is what differs
steps.body: A linear model ADDS the same $m$ every step, forever. An exponential MULTIPLIES, so its step is a fraction of a growing total — and therefore grows too. Once its step exceeds $m$, it gains ground every step and never gives any back.

steps.title: Who leads here?
steps.prompt: Compare $L(x) = 500x$ and $E(x) = 2^{x}$ at $x = 10$. Which is larger?
steps.explanation: $L(10) = 5000$ while $E(10) = 1024$ — the line leads by nearly five to one. But check further out: at $x = 20$, $L = 10\,000$ and $E = 1\,048\,576$. The exponential has not merely caught up, it is a hundred times ahead. Leading at $x = 10$ says nothing about the long run.

steps.title: Why the doubling wage sounds absurd
steps.body: Day $20$ of the doubling job pays $524\,288$₮ — still less than the flat million. Day $31$ pays over a BILLION. Eleven days turned a losing offer into a fortune, and nothing in the first twenty days hinted at it. This is why exponential growth is the single most under-estimated pattern in mathematics.

steps.title: Which model does a situation need?
steps.body: Ask what stays the same from one step to the next. A fixed QUANTITY — $900$₮ a kilometre, $4$ cm an hour — is linear. A fixed PROPORTION of the current total — $7\%$ a year — is exponential.
beats: Both say "per" — read what follows it
A unit means linear; a percent sign means exponential

steps.title: Which model fits?
steps.prompt: A savings account pays $5\%$ interest a year on the balance. Which model?
options: Linear, because the rate is fixed
Exponential, because the increase is a percent of a growing balance
Linear, because interest is added each year
Neither — it needs a new kind of model
steps.explanation: Five percent of a growing balance is a growing amount, so the increase is not constant. On $1000$: year one adds $50$, year two adds $52.50$, year three adds $55.13$. Constant percent means exponential — $B = P(1.05)^{t}$.

steps.title: Locate the crossover by table, not by algebra
steps.body: Solving $2^{x} = 1000x$ exactly needs logarithms, which arrive in IM2. Here, try values until the winner flips, then narrow. "Between $x = 13$ and $x = 14$" is the expected answer — and it is genuinely useful.

steps.title: What you now own
points: An exponential with $b > 1$ eventually exceeds **any** linear function
It can start far behind — the slope of the line changes only the timing
Why: the line's step is fixed, the curve's step grows
Constant amount → linear; constant percent → exponential
Find the crossover by table or graph; the algebra waits for IM2

lessons.title: Building an Exponential Model
lessons.concreteComparison: A doctor knows a drug's concentration halves every four hours and that a dose starts at $200$ mg. From those two facts alone she can predict the level at any future hour — and decide when the next dose is safe. Two data points is all an exponential model needs, and this lesson is how to extract it from them.
lessons.objective: Construct $y = a \cdot b^{x}$ from a description, a table, or two data points; handle doubling time and half-life; and use the model to predict and to solve backwards by table.
concept: **From a description, read the two numbers off.** "Starts at $8000$ and grows $5\%$ a year" gives $a = 8000$ and $b = 1.05$ immediately. Most modelling questions in IM1 are this direct, and the only real skill is converting the percent to the factor correctly.

**From a table.** The starting value is the output at zero and the base is the ratio. If the table includes $x = 0$, that output IS $a$. Then divide any output by the one before it to get $b$ — and check the ratio is the same for every consecutive pair, or the model does not apply at all.

**From two points that skip steps.** Given $(0, 5)$ and $(3, 40)$, the value has multiplied by $\frac{40}{5} = 8$ over THREE steps, so $b^{3} = 8$ and $b = 2$. Take the appropriate root of the total factor — that is the general move whenever the data points are not adjacent.

**Doubling time and half-life are the same idea.** "Doubles every $6$ hours" means the factor is $2$ per six hours, so with $t$ in hours the model is $y = a \cdot 2^{\,t/6}$. "Halves every $4$ hours" gives $y = a \cdot \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t/4}$. Dividing the exponent by the period converts the clock into a count of periods, which is what the base expects.

**Check the model against every data point you were given.** Fit it using two, then test it on the rest. A model that reproduces the data it was built from and fails everything else is not a model — and this check costs one line per point.

**Solve backwards by table.** "When does the population reach $10\,000$?" cannot be solved algebraically without logarithms. Compute values until you bracket the target, then state the interval: "between year $8$ and year $9$". That is the honest and expected IM1 answer.
lessons.keyIdea: $a$ is the value at $x = 0$; $b$ is the factor per step, found by dividing consecutive values — or by taking the $n$-th root when the points are $n$ steps apart. Check the finished model on every data point.

facts.title: From two adjacent points
facts.explanation: Divide consecutive outputs. Confirm the ratio repeats before trusting it.

facts.title: From points n steps apart
facts.explanation: The total factor spread over n steps. Take the n-th root.

facts.title: Doubling time and half-life
facts.explanation: Divide the elapsed time by the period, turning a clock reading into a count of periods.

workedExamples.statement: A table shows $(0, 6), (1, 18), (2, 54), (3, 162)$. Build the exponential model and predict the value at $x = 6$.
workedExamples.solution: **The starting value.** The table includes $x = 0$, so $a = 6$.**The base.** Divide consecutive outputs — and check the ratio repeats:$$\frac{18}{6} = 3, \qquad \frac{54}{18} = 3, \qquad \frac{162}{54} = 3.$$Constant, so $b = 3$.**The model.**$$y = 6 \cdot 3^{x}.$$**Check on every given point.** $y(1) = 18$ ✓, $y(2) = 54$ ✓, $y(3) = 162$ ✓ — the model reproduces all four, not just the two it was built from.**Predict.**$$y(6) = 6 \cdot 3^{6} = 6 \times 729 = 4374.$$

workedExamples.statement: An exponential model passes through $(0, 5)$ and $(3, 40)$. Find $b$ and write the model.
workedExamples.solution: **The starting value comes free.** The point at $x = 0$ gives $a = 5$.**The total factor over three steps.**$$\frac{40}{5} = 8.$$That $8$ is $b$ applied THREE times, not once:$$b^{3} = 8 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad b = \sqrt[3]{8} = 2.$$**The model.**$$y = 5 \cdot 2^{x}.$$**Check both given points.** $y(0) = 5$ ✓ and $y(3) = 5 \times 8 = 40$ ✓**The trap.** Taking $b = 8$ would give $y(3) = 5 \times 512 = 2560$, wildly wrong. When two points are $n$ steps apart, the ratio between them is $b^{n}$, and you must take the $n$-th root.

workedExamples.statement: A drug's concentration starts at $200$ mg and halves every $4$ hours. Write the model and find the concentration after $10$ hours.
workedExamples.solution: **Set up the period.** The factor is $\frac{1}{2}$ per FOUR hours, so with $t$ in hours the exponent must count periods, not hours:$$C(t) = 200 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t/4}.$$**Check the period.** At $t = 4$: $200 \times \frac{1}{2} = 100$ ✓, halved as promised. At $t = 8$: $200 \times \frac{1}{4} = 50$ ✓**After 10 hours.** That is $\frac{10}{4} = 2.5$ half-lives:$$C(10) = 200 \times \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2.5} = 200 \times 0.176777 = 35.36\ \text{mg}.$$**Sanity-check the size.** Ten hours is between two half-lives ($50$ mg) and three ($25$ mg), so an answer of $35.4$ mg sits sensibly between them ✓**Why divide the exponent.** Writing $200 \cdot (0.5)^{10}$ would treat ten HOURS as ten halvings and give $0.195$ mg — off by a factor of nearly two hundred.

workedExamples.statement: A town's population was $18\,000$ in $2015$ and $22\,500$ in $2020$. Assuming exponential growth, find the annual rate and predict $2030$.
workedExamples.solution: **Set the clock.** Let $t$ be years since $2015$, so $a = 18\,000$ and the second reading is at $t = 5$.**Total factor over five years.**$$\frac{22\,500}{18\,000} = 1.25.$$**Annual factor.** That growth is spread over five years:$$b^{5} = 1.25 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad b = \sqrt[5]{1.25} \approx 1.0456.$$So the town grows about $4.56\%$ a year.**Check.** $18\,000 \times 1.0456^{5} = 18\,000 \times 1.25 = 22\,500$ ✓**Predict 2030** — that is $t = 15$, three of the five-year periods:$$P(15) = 18\,000 \times (1.25)^{3} = 18\,000 \times 1.953125 = 35\,156.25,$$about $35\,156$ people.**The caveat.** This extrapolates ten years past the data on the assumption that the growth rate holds. Towns change — a factory closes, a road opens — so the prediction is what the MODEL says, and any answer worth full marks says so.

commonMistakes.text: Using the ratio between two points that are several steps apart as b.
commonMistakes.correction: From (0, 5) to (3, 40) the total factor is 8 over three steps, so b = ∛8 = 2. Taking b = 8 overshoots enormously.

commonMistakes.text: Writing y = a·(0.5)ᵗ for a quantity that halves every 4 hours.
commonMistakes.correction: Divide the exponent by the period: y = a·(0.5)^(t/4). Otherwise every hour is treated as a full half-life.

commonMistakes.text: Fitting to two points and never checking the rest of the data.
commonMistakes.correction: Any two points determine a model. Testing the others is what shows the model actually fits — and costs one line per point.

commonMistakes.text: Reporting a long extrapolation with no caveat.
commonMistakes.correction: A model fitted to five years of data and pushed out fifteen assumes the rate held throughout. Say so — it is part of the answer.

tryIt.statement: Build the model for the table $(0, 4), (1, 12), (2, 36)$ and find $y(5)$.
tryIt.solution: $a = 4$ from the value at zero; ratios $\frac{12}{4} = \frac{36}{12} = 3$ give $b = 3$. So $y = 4 \cdot 3^{x}$, and $y(5) = 4 \times 243 = 972$.

tryIt.statement: An exponential model passes through $(0, 7)$ and $(2, 63)$. Find $b$.
tryIt.solution: The total factor is $\frac{63}{7} = 9$ over two steps, so $b^{2} = 9$ and $b = 3$. The model is $y = 7 \cdot 3^{x}$, and checking: $7 \times 9 = 63$ ✓

tryIt.statement: A sample of $80$ g decays with a half-life of $6$ years. Write the model and find the mass after $18$ years.
tryIt.solution: $M(t) = 80 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t/6}$. After $18$ years that is $\frac{18}{6} = 3$ half-lives, so $M = 80 \times \frac{1}{8} = 10$ g.

steps.title: From a description, the model reads itself
steps.body: "Starts at $8000$, grows $5\%$ a year" is already $a = 8000$ and $b = 1.05$. The only place to go wrong is the percent-to-factor step — and Lesson 1 settled that.
beats: Write $y = a \cdot b^{x}$ and check at $x = 0$

steps.title: The value at zero, and the repeating ratio
steps.body: If the table has $x = 0$, that output IS $a$. Divide consecutive outputs for $b$ — and confirm the ratio is the SAME every time, or the data is not exponential and none of this applies.

steps.title: Points several steps apart need a root
steps.body: From $(0, 5)$ to $(3, 40)$ the value multiplied by $8$ — but over THREE steps. So $b^{3} = 8$ and $b = 2$. Whenever the data points are $n$ apart, take the $n$-th root of the total factor.
beats: Then check the model on both points

steps.title: Find the base
steps.prompt: An exponential passes through $(0, 3)$ and $(4, 48)$. What is $b$?
steps.explanation: The total factor is $\frac{48}{3} = 16$, spread over FOUR steps, so $b^{4} = 16$ and $b = 2$. Check: $3 \cdot 2^{4} = 3 \times 16 = 48$ ✓. Answering $16$ treats the whole growth as one step and would predict $3 \cdot 16^{4} = 196\,608$ at $x = 4$.

steps.title: Doubling time and half-life divide the exponent
steps.body: "Doubles every $6$ hours" is a factor of $2$ per six hours, so the exponent must count SIX-HOUR PERIODS: $y = a \cdot 2^{\,t/6}$. Dividing by the period converts a clock reading into the count the base expects.

steps.title: A drug with a four-hour half-life
Which model is right?
steps.prompt: A sample halves every $5$ years and starts at $60$ g. Which model gives the mass after $t$ years?
steps.explanation: The exponent must count five-year periods, so divide $t$ by $5$. Check at $t = 5$: $60 \times (0.5)^{1} = 30$ g — halved, as required ✓. Option A would halve every YEAR, giving $1.875$ g at $t = 5$ instead of $30$.

steps.title: A town, fitted from two census figures
Solve backwards with a table
steps.body: "When does it reach $10\,000$?" needs logarithms to solve exactly, and those arrive in IM2. Compute values until you bracket the target and report the interval — "between year $8$ and year $9$" is a complete IM1 answer.

steps.title: What you now own
points: $a$ is the value at $x = 0$; $b$ is the factor per step
Points $n$ steps apart: take the $n$-th root of the total factor
Doubling time or half-life $T$ → divide the exponent by $T$
Check the finished model against **every** data point you were given
Solve backwards by table, and state the bracketing interval

practice.statement: A population of $12\,000$ grows $4\%$ a year. Write the model and find the population after $3$ years.
A machine worth $6\,000\,000$₮ loses $20\%$ of its value each year. Find its value after $3$ years.
practice.solution: Keeping $80\%$ gives a factor of $0.8$: $V(3) = 6\,000\,000 \times 0.512 = 3\,072\,000$₮. Note this is not a $60\%$ loss — it retains $51.2\%$.
Differences are $4, 4, 4$ — constant, so it is **linear** with slope $4$ and intercept $9$: $y = 4x + 9$. Check at $x = 3$: $12 + 9 = 21$ ✓
Differences $8, 40, 200$ are not constant; ratios $\frac{10}{2} = \frac{50}{10} = \frac{250}{50} = 5$ are. So it is **exponential**: $y = 2 \cdot 5^{x}$. Check at $x = 3$: $2 \times 125 = 250$ ✓

practice.statement: For $y = 8 \cdot 2^{x}$, give the $y$-intercept and the values at $x = 3$ and $x = -2$.
practice.solution: The intercept is $8$. At $x = 3$: $8 \times 8 = 64$. At $x = -2$: $8 \times \frac{1}{4} = 2$ — positive, as every output of this function is.

practice.statement: Describe the end behaviour and asymptote of $y = 40 \cdot (0.25)^{x}$.
practice.solution: The base is below $1$, so this is decay: as $x \to \infty$ the output approaches $0$, making $y = 0$ a horizontal asymptote; as $x \to -\infty$ it grows without bound. Check: $y(4) = 40 \times 0.0039 = 0.156$, and $y(-2) = 40 \times 16 = 640$.

practice.statement: Build the exponential model through $(0, 3)$ and $(2, 27)$.
practice.solution: $a = 3$. The total factor is $\frac{27}{3} = 9$ over two steps, so $b^{2} = 9$ and $b = 3$. The model is $y = 3 \cdot 3^{x}$. Check: $3 \times 9 = 27$ ✓

practice.statement: A culture doubles every $3$ hours from $500$ cells. Write the model and find the count after $12$ hours.
practice.solution: $N(t) = 500 \cdot 2^{\,t/3}$. After $12$ hours that is $4$ doublings: $500 \times 16 = 8000$ cells.

practice.statement: Compare $L(x) = 60x$ with $E(x) = 3^{x}$ at $x = 3, 5$ and $7$. Where is the crossover?
practice.solution: At $x = 3$: $L = 180$, $E = 27$ — the line leads. At $x = 5$: $L = 300$, $E = 243$ — still the line, barely. At $x = 7$: $L = 420$, $E = 2187$ — the curve has won. Checking $x = 6$: $L = 360$, $E = 729$ — already won, so the crossover is between $x = 5$ and $x = 6$.

practice.statement: Classify each: (a) a courier charging $1200$₮ per kilogram; (b) a savings account at $8\%$ a year; (c) a candle burning $3$ cm an hour.
practice.solution: (a) **Linear** — a constant amount per kilogram. (b) **Exponential** — a constant percent of a changing balance. (c) **Linear** — a constant amount per hour.

practice.statement: A sample of $240$ g has a half-life of $8$ days. How much remains after $24$ days?
practice.solution: $24$ days is $\frac{24}{8} = 3$ half-lives, so the mass is $240 \times \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{3} = 240 \times \frac{1}{8} = 30$ g.

practice.statement: A quantity grows $15\%$ then falls $15\%$. What is the net change?
practice.solution: Multiply the factors: $1.15 \times 0.85 = 0.9775$. The quantity ends at $97.75\%$ of where it started — a net LOSS of $2.25\%$, not a return to the start. The rise was taken on the smaller number and the fall on the larger one.

testYourself.statement: A town of $25\,000$ grows $6\%$ a year. Write the model, find the population after $4$ years, and explain why the answer is not a $24\%$ increase.
testYourself.solution: **Model.** Growing $6\%$ keeps everything and adds six percent, so $b = 1.06$:$$P(t) = 25\,000 \cdot (1.06)^{t}.$$Check the start: $P(0) = 25\,000$ ✓**After 4 years.**$$1.06^{4} = 1.26247696, \qquad P(4) = 25\,000 \times 1.26247696 = 31\,561.924,$$about $31\,562$ people.**Why the rates do not simply add.** Four years at $6\%$ produces a $26.25\%$ increase, not $4 \times 6 = 24\%$. Each year's growth is computed on the previous year's larger population, so the extra growth compounds. The linear answer would have been $25\,000 \times 1.24 = 31\,000$ — about $562$ people short.

**Table A — differences.**$$85 - 100 = -15, \quad 70 - 85 = -15, \quad 55 - 70 = -15.$$Constant, so **linear** with slope $-15$: $y = 100 - 15x$. Check at $x = 3$: $100 - 45 = 55$ ✓**Table B — differences.**$$-15, \quad -12.75, \quad -10.8375.$$Not constant. **Ratios:**$$\frac{85}{100} = 0.85, \quad \frac{72.25}{85} = 0.85, \quad \frac{61.4125}{72.25} = 0.85.$$Constant, so **exponential**: $y = 100 \cdot (0.85)^{x}$, a $15\%$ decay per step.**The instructive contrast.** Both start at $100$ and both drop by $15$ on the first step. A tells you a fixed $15$ leaves every time; B tells you $15\%$ leaves every time, which is a shrinking amount. Table A reaches zero at $x = \frac{20}{3}$; table B never does.

testYourself.statement: For $y = 6 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{x}$, give the $y$-intercept, the values at $x = 2$ and $x = -2$, the asymptote, and the end behaviour.
testYourself.solution: **Intercept.** At $x = 0$: $y = 6 \cdot 1 = 6$, so $(0, 6)$.**Two steps right.** $6 \times \frac{1}{9} = \frac{2}{3}$.**Two steps left.** A negative exponent flips the fraction: $6 \times 3^{2} = 54$. Positive and large — the curve climbs steeply to the left.**Asymptote.** $y = 0$. Since $6$ and $\frac{1}{3}$ are both positive, every output is positive, so the curve never touches the horizontal axis.**End behaviour.** The base is below $1$, so as $x \to \infty$ the output approaches $0$; as $x \to -\infty$ it grows without bound.

testYourself.statement: An exponential model passes through $(0, 4)$ and $(3, 108)$. Find $b$, write the model, and predict $y(5)$.
testYourself.solution: **Starting value.** The point at $x = 0$ gives $a = 4$.**Total factor over three steps.**$$\frac{108}{4} = 27.$$**Annual factor.** That is $b$ applied three times:$$b^{3} = 27 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad b = \sqrt[3]{27} = 3.$$**Model.**$$y = 4 \cdot 3^{x}.$$**Check both given points.** $y(0) = 4$ ✓ and $y(3) = 4 \times 27 = 108$ ✓**Predict.**$$y(5) = 4 \times 3^{5} = 4 \times 243 = 972.$$

testYourself.statement: A radioactive sample of $500$ g has a half-life of $12$ years. Write the model, find the mass after $36$ years, and after $18$ years.
testYourself.solution: **Model.** The factor is $\frac{1}{2}$ per twelve years, so the exponent counts twelve-year periods:$$M(t) = 500 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t/12}.$$**After 36 years.** That is $\frac{36}{12} = 3$ half-lives:$$M(36) = 500 \times \frac{1}{8} = 62.5\ \text{g}.$$**After 18 years.** That is $1.5$ half-lives:$$M(18) = 500 \times \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{1.5} = 500 \times 0.353553 = 176.78\ \text{g}.$$**Sanity check.** Eighteen years lies between one half-life ($250$ g) and two ($125$ g), and $176.8$ g sits between them ✓**Why the model never reaches zero.** Each period removes half of what remains, so the mass approaches zero without arriving — the horizontal asymptote made physical.

testYourself.statement: Plan A pays $2\,000\,000$₮ now and adds $150\,000$₮ each year. Plan B pays $1\,200\,000$₮ now and grows $15\%$ each year. Compare at years $3$, $8$ and $15$, and advise someone choosing for a $20$-year horizon.
testYourself.solution: **Models.**$$A(t) = 2\,000\,000 + 150\,000t, \qquad B(t) = 1\,200\,000 \cdot (1.15)^{t}.$$**Year 3.** $A = 2\,450\,000$; $B = 1\,200\,000 \times 1.520875 = 1\,825\,050$. **A leads.****Year 8.** $A = 3\,200\,000$; $B = 1\,200\,000 \times 3.0590 = 3\,670\,844$. **B leads** — it has overtaken between years $3$ and $8$.**Year 15.** $A = 4\,250\,000$; $B = 1\,200\,000 \times 8.1371 = 9\,764\,502$. **B leads decisively**, by more than double.**Advice for 20 years.** Choose B. At year $20$, $A = 5\,000\,000$ while $B = 1\,200\,000 \times 16.3665 = 19\,639\,844$ — nearly four times as much. A starts higher and is more predictable, but a fixed annual addition cannot compete with compounding over two decades. The crossover falls between years $6$ and $7$, so any horizon past about seven years favours B.

testYourself.statement: A lake's fish population was $8000$ in $2018$ and $5120$ in $2021$. Assuming exponential decay, find the annual factor and percent loss, predict $2024$, and comment on the prediction.
testYourself.solution: **Set the clock.** Let $t$ be years since $2018$, so $a = 8000$ and the second reading is at $t = 3$.**Total factor over three years.**$$\frac{5120}{8000} = 0.64.$$**Annual factor.**$$b^{3} = 0.64 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad b = \sqrt[3]{0.64} \approx 0.8618.$$So the population keeps about $86.2\%$ each year, losing about $13.8\%$ annually.**Check.** $8000 \times 0.64 = 5120$ ✓ at $t = 3$.**Predict 2024** — that is $t = 6$, two of the three-year periods:$$P(6) = 8000 \times (0.64)^{2} = 8000 \times 0.4096 = 3276.8,$$about $3277$ fish.**Comment.** The model assumes the same decay rate continues for three more years beyond the data. A lake population may stabilise as competition eases, or crash faster if the cause worsens — so $3277$ is what the MODEL predicts, not a measurement. Two data points also cannot distinguish exponential decay from several other shapes that pass through the same pair; more readings would be needed to justify the choice of model.
